rescind

rih-SIND · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To rescind is to officially cancel or revoke something.

Facing public backlash, the university quickly rescinded its plan to raise tuition mid-semester.

Example

When the manufacturer discovered a dangerous defect, it moved to rescind every warranty exception it had previously granted for that model.

To rescind is to formally take back or cancel something you had officially put in place -- a law, an offer, a policy, or a decision.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

revoke: To revoke is to officially take back something that was granted -- a license, a permit, a privilege. Rescind is nearly its twin, but it points at decisions and rules: offers, policies, and orders get rescinded. Revoke pulls back a permission someone held; rescind unmakes a decision an institution made.

annul: To annul is to declare a formal act -- a marriage, a contract, an election -- legally void, as if it had never happened. To rescind is to take back a decision going forward: the offer or policy really existed, and now it is cancelled. Annulment erases the past; rescinding stops the future.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

enact: to make something into law or official policy

ratify: to formally approve or confirm something

Where it sits · how completely and widely it is undone

adjust → rescind → abolish

adjust vs. rescind: To adjust a rule is only to tweak it, leaving it alive in changed form -- far short of rescind, which cancels the decision outright.

abolish vs. rescind: To abolish goes further than rescind: rescinding cancels one decision or policy, while abolishing wipes out an entire practice or system, usually for good.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — re-: back (Latin)

root — scind: to cut, to split (from Latin scindere)

Put it together: Rescind is built from re- ('back') + scind ('to cut, to split,' from Latin scindere) -- literally 'to cut back,' which fits perfectly: to rescind something is to cut it off, cancelling what was previously in effect.

Use the root in a new word: scissors: She used the kitchen scissors to snip the stubborn plastic packaging open.

Word Building

Word Choice

Rescind is a formal word, most common in legal, political, or official contexts -- laws, licenses, offers, and policies get rescinded, not casual plans between friends. Compare it with renege (breaking a personal promise) and repudiate (formally rejecting a claim or belief) -- all three share the same 'going back' idea, but rescind is reserved for official, institutional actions.
